newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Zinc prices extend gains, gold languishes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Zinc prices extend gains, gold languishes.

text.p: World zinc prices pierced a key psychological barrier on Friday to hit their highest for nearly seven years as speculators bought heavily on dwindling world stocks.
Gold, by contrast, was driven to four-month lows in London by increasingly negative sentiment in a market that remains worried about possible central bank sales.
Zinc's run-up has been fuelled by investors seeking to capitalise on a healthy global economy by betting on a base metal with low producer and consumer stocks.

Inventory levels of zinc, which is used to galvanise steel and alloyed with copper to make brass, continue to fall at the London Metal Exchange (LME), where they have fallen by 15 percent since the start of the year.

But analysts have cautioned against the pace and extent of the price rise, warning that the market may have outpaced fundamentals. Zinc peaked at $1,405 a tonne, before settling back from the key $1,400 level in late LME trade to close at $1,399, up $6.

In other industrial base metals, nickel sprang into action in the late morning, breaking above $7,200 on pessimism about a speedy resolution to a work stoppage at one of Inco's major Canadian units. Union officials there said they did not expect any developments until after a July maintenance closure.
Copper languished on a recent reversal in sentiment following the metal's failure to break through $2,600.
Among precious metals, palladium and platinum notched higher, with no sign of shipments resuming from Russia, which had said it would begin exports again on Friday.
Russia supplies 60 percent of world palladium needs and about 25 percent of platinum, but has been out the market since December because of internal wrangling over control of its metals industry.

Elsewhere, cocoa settled back to consolidate Thursday's sharp overnight gains, dipping into negative territory. Traders await the bi-weekly Commitment of Traders report due after New York's close, with expectations it will show a sharp increase in speculative long positions, which could make the market vulnerable to a sell-off.
Coffee was subdued amid continuing signs of warm weather in Brazil's coffee belt. London September robusta futures ended the day $5 down at $1,855 a tonne.
Signs of a bumper U.S. harvest continued to weight on grain markets, with July Chicago Board of Trade wheat futures trading slightly lower after sagging to a fresh 4-1/2 month low on Thursday.
Crude oil dropped on general market negativity with little concern about the approaching OPEC meeting in Vienna, which is expected to do nothing to curb quota violations.

Estimates from OPEC headquarters showed that in the remainder of 1997 its 11 members would produce one million barrels a day more than was needed to satisfy world demand. While a handful of Gulf producers led by Saudi Arabia have maintained quota discipline, others like Venezuela and Nigeria have been pumping at full steam without regard to oil prices.
London Brent for August delivery was down 21 cents at $17.58.
